utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 3rd of March, 2009. I would like to greet Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Pusic, as well as all the attorneys, and to Mr. Karnavas, who's back again today, all the representatives of the OTP, and the witness, who will answer the questions of the Prosecutor in a few moments as part of the cross-examination. Before that, I need to turn to the Registrar, because we need an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. 6D has submitted a list of objections to documents tendered by the Prosecution through Witness Ante Kvesic. This document shall be given Exhibit IC 936. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Witness, insofar as the Bench controls examination and cross-examination, I would like to tell you that we want this to run as smoothly as possible, and you were a little bit emotional yesterday. So you are going to be put questions by the Prosecutor as part of the cross-examination. This is usually a rather difficult time, because rests on the Prosecution the burden of proof. The Prosecutor may put leading questions to you and may challenge your credibility, so this can be a difficult moment for you. This is something I wanted to tell you so that you're not taken by surprise. In addition, since you belong to the medical profession, wait before you answer, breathe heavily if you need to, take in your breath if you need to. I know that these can be very challenging and difficult moments. This is what I wanted to tell you. I hope you had a good rest last night, and I hope you are able to start this cross-examination in the best conditions. I would like to greet you once again, and, Prosecutor, you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and all those in around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And good morning to you, sir. I want to ask you about what you saw in the HVO detention camps that you visited. All right? Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but what I saw -- yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What you saw, and what you heard there, and what you learnt about the HVO detention camps. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question? The war is full of information, misinformation, and what you hear doesn't mean that that was what actually happened, so you can't talk about it unless you check it out. Only then is your testimony valid and has any specific weight, because if I were to tell you everything that I had heard about, well, I mean, I'd be here for 500 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We don't want that, sir, so we'll stick --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, answer the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. The Bench will assess the probative value of your answers to the questions that are put to you. Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When you gave evidence to this Court in the Tuta Stela case, you were asked a question by counsel representing one of the defendants, you were asked if you could please tell the Court everything that you knew about the Heliodrom, all right, and you replied that the Heliodrom was, and I'm going to quote your words exactly: "The Heliodrom was for me, personally, a very unpleasant experience." All right? And that's right, isn't it, it was a very unpleasant experience for you to go into the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And we saw yesterday that you became quite upset when you were asked to remember the things that you had seen both there and elsewhere; is that also right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And can I ask you a question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, that's not really how it works here, sir, no. Just going back to what we have just been talking about, you found it upsetting to recall what you saw, and I want, if I can, to try to understand why that might be. All right? And I want to try, if I can, to do that without upsetting you unnecessarily, but I need to ask you what you saw and what it was like in those places. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we start, please, with your first visit to the Heliodrom, which you told the Court yesterday took place in mid-May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In fact, I think I'm right in saying that we can do better than that; that you told the Trial Chamber in Tuta Stela that you'd gone into the Heliodrom on the 11th and 12th of May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the middle of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. You had been asked to go there because you had been told that a large number of people had been detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you had been asked to go there to help to ensure that their detention didn't involve the outbreak of epidemics; yeah?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When you got there, you saw that there were indeed a very large number of people who had just been detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: People from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You knew some --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the majority, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Of course, you would only know a proportion, but people from Mostar who were suddenly in a detention centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to add something to that. Your Honours, as a doctor myself, I know people who come to hospital, so my -- the circle of people that I know is far greater and doesn't only relate to Mostar, and it's quite logical that I know the people of Mostar better because I was born there and lived there, but I don't want you to understand that I know only people from Mostar. I know people whom I treated, I know their families, friends, so my circle of acquaintances is much, much larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So you recognised more people than the average citizen might have recognised in the Heliodrom on the 11th and the 12th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did you ask them what was going on and why they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of them did not know. Well, if I was there yesterday -- or, rather, if I was stressed yesterday, I was under even greater stress before, so you can imagine what the people who were there felt like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you're comparing your stress yesterday, giving evidence here, to the stress of the people who were imprisoned and didn't know the reason on the 11th and 12th of May; is that what we're to understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you need to understand is this: That as far as I'm concerned, stress -- let me give you an example. I don't remember the link at all when I was here and when my distinguished counsel asked -- when I asked her what the time was, she said, "February." And I said, "Ms. Nozica, it can't have been February, because it was warm, the weather was warm." So I tried to push that out of my mind. But you cannot conclude that my stress was equal to their stress. Their stress was enormous, much greater than my own stress. Now, if I, as a human being, as a man of such and such an age, as an individual with a great deal of education, as somebody who has travelled the world, experienced stress, then I can only imagine how much greater their stress was, and that it triggered a stress reaction where a large number of people cannot remember things. But I was quite definite and certain that they weren't there of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I think we're not going to disagree about that at all, and I'm going to ask you, if you can, to focus on the questions. I know it's difficult. We accept that you've travelled the world and that you're a very well-educated man. We take that for granted. All right? I'm not asking you about your autobiography at the moment. I'm asking you about conditions in the Heliodrom, and I understand you to be saying that the people that you saw on the 11th and 12th of May were unaware, many of them, why they were there, and as a result they were highly distressed. Do I have that position accurately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, you've understood that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question for you. I listened to the questions of the Prosecutor very carefully, and you have answered this question. You said that those people who were there did not know why they had been detained, and it's very easy to visualise the situation. When you left the Heliodrom, did you tell your superiors, "I am going to the prison, I am going to the Heliodrom. I have met people whom I knew, and these people didn't know why they had been detained." Did you tell that to your superiors, and if you did, what did they then tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, of course I did tell them, and that was my duty. It was my duty to tell them. And when I went down there, as you've already heard -- well, Dr. Bagaric told me to go down there. And as far as I was concerned, as an individual dealing with preventive medicine, any meeting, or rally, or collection of people generally, refugees, displaced persons, or whatever, are places where I -- where my duty would take me. But when I saw the situation there, I understood, as a doctor, that people were under stress, that they were afraid, and that many of them who knew me, and I was in uniform at the time, they saw me as being someone from the other side, not as a doctor. And I don't hold that against them. Later on, that changed, and I did go up there, and I told them straight away: "As far as I'm concerned, I see that as a prison. There are too many people in one place. We have to do something about it because infectious diseases will break out." And when I asked them why they were there - that was your question, was it not, Your Honour? - then the answer that I was given, roughly, was that they were there for security reasons, safety reasons. And if you'll allow me to say, Your Honour, on the 9th of September -- on the 9th of May, 1992, when that unfortunate conflict began, I was in my flat. I didn't know about the conflict at all, although I was a member, as you know, of the staff, and I came to the new hospital which is at a distance of several kilometres. I went there by car. I was in a police car, because the police station is across the road from me and there was shooting all over the place. And I was told that it was for these reasons, because the war had begun, because we had been attacked by the Muslim armed forces, and that's why they were there, for those reasons. So that's what I knew. And as a former soldier, myself, or, rather, as a member of the army, there might have been another example, like the 5th Column, but I wasn't interested in that, as a doctor. All I was interested in was to see what we could do to prevent an epidemic from breaking out. So I go back to yesterday, and, please, I was the chief of the Service for Preventive Medicine, that's all. All I was interested in was how to prevent and stop infectious diseases from breaking out, or, rather, if they did occur sporadically, to prevent them from becoming an epidemic, so that was my prime concern. And I consider that in that aspect -- or, rather, that was the work that I had to do, and I think that my work had a humanitarian character in doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Sir, that, if you'll forgive me for saying so, was a very long answer. The question that you had been asked by the President of this Trial Chamber was whether you told your superiors, and I think you started by saying, yes, you told Dr. Bagaric what was going on at the Heliodrom. Yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, I have to explain the conditions so that Their Honours can understand, because I'm in the hands of justice here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for a moment. We are going to look at the conditions, I assure you, but I want to stick with one question at a time and then we won't, I hope, become confused. You were asked a question, and it's a question that I want to repeat and give you a third opportunity to answer. Who did you tell? You've said Dr. Bagaric. Who else did you tell about what you'd seen in the Heliodrom that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Sector for Health, so the people who were in the Health Sector. Yes, the Health Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So the people in the Health Sector of the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. In later visits to the Heliodrom, did you also see that there was a wide age range of detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you look with me, please, at a document in the bundle in front of you that's labelled P 05328, P 05328. Perhaps if the usher might be prepared to lend some assistance. I think you have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This is a document that is dated the 23rd of September of 1993, and we can see that it's a list of detainees who were brought in to the Heliodrom on the 21st of September of 1993. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And we know, sir, that you went into the Heliodrom on the 30th of September, some nine days after these detainees are recorded as having arrived. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have a document stating that, then that is probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we do. It's one of your reports, and we'll look at it in due course, but it's dated the 30th of September. That's the day that you went into the Heliodrom. All right? If we just look at this list together, at number 5 we have a name and a date of birth of the 2nd of April of 1980. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So that individual would have been, I think, 13 in 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a moment, and I assure you, I'll give you a chance to say what you want to say. If you turn the page and look at the last name, number 36, apparently born on the 5th of July of 1922, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That individual would have been 71 at the time that you went into the Heliodrom on the 30th of September; all right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So just to try to get a picture of what you were experiencing in the Heliodrom, in terms of the people who were there, before we look at the conditions, just the people who were there, they were people who were as young as 13 and as old as 71; is that right? Was that your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make myself understood. This list was written by Mr. Stanko Bozic. I don't know him [as interpreted], but I'm quite sure that I saw people of different ages. For example, under number 27, "Omer (Osman) Terzic," you'll see later on that he was involved with the medical corps to work as a technician in the infirmary. So I saw this large span, age span, but I'm disgusted when I see that somebody was 13 years old. That is terrible, impossible, but I didn't see anybody like that. Had I seen somebody of that age, I would have recorded it straight away and informed people straight away, because I'm a father myself and know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. I think the translation that I heard was that you didn't know Stanko Bozic, but in fact you dealt with Stanko Bozic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did know him, I knew him very well, sir. I knew him very well, Mr. Prosecutor, but I hadn't received -- I didn't receive this list. I don't know whom this list is addressed to; not to me. The Health Sector, maybe, but not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It may just be an error in the translation. Our translation says: "This list was written by Mr. Stanko Bozic. I don't know him, but I'm quite sure ..." I just wanted to clarify that. You knew who Stanko Bozic was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, in preparing this case, you probably noticed, and I spoke about this yesterday and you were sitting down, so you could have heard me say that the plan for my work was always uniform, always the same, and that in the first part it would say who was present. And you could have noticed that Mr. Bozic was always recorded as being present, and it would have been a terrible lie to say that I did not know the man, and I contacted him. Every time when I arrived at that locality, I tried to find Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that she heard the witness say, "No," so I was mistaken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You and I are not disagreeing. It was a mistake that happened in the translation. There's nothing at all for you to worry about. I wanted to clarify it so that the record is clear, because you knew Stanko Bozic, and we both agreed about that. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then turn, please, with me to another report that we have, not written by you, but dealing with two of the same detention centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to another document: We have understood that you were an officer of the JNA. This is what you told us. Yesterday, I understood that you had some understanding of military affairs. When we see this document, there's no shadow of a doubt that you were not the addressee of this document, but on seeing this document, you see "Central Military Prison," and you see the name of a young person who is 13. This is an issue, in military terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, terrible, just terrible. A 13-year-old child can't be a soldier. "Mr. Hasan [indiscernible], Music, 71," he can't be a soldier. Theoretically, he can work somewhere, answering a telephone, for example, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the case of 71 is concerned, some people are 71 and still very busy. Maybe it's not so easy for a person who is 71. Some people at 71 are judges, even. So at 71, you still have quite a lot of energy and have enough energy. But a 13-year-old, well, that's not the same, and his name shouldn't have been on there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The report I wanted to look at with you, sir, is -- in your bundle, it's P 06729. I wonder if you'd find that for us, please. It's further on in the bundle than the one you've just looked at, P 06729. This is a report that we're going to look at --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number did you say, 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This is a report that we're going to look at a little bit in the course of the morning. It's a report prepared by the Security and Information Service of the Military Police Sector in relation to the work of Gabela and the Heliodrom Detention Centres. Can you see that report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, inspection and supervision, yes, for Gabela and Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And we're still on the topic, sir, to assist you, we're still on the topic of who was in the Heliodrom, all right, before we look at what was happening to them, who was actually there. Do you follow my questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am following.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this -- how can I have anything to do with SIS? The SIS followed me. As a former JNA officer, I was under SIS supervision, surveillance, and I don't see what I have to do with this particular SIS, because I was under surveillance by SIS because I was the persona non grata for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, it would be very helpful for the Court if you would just answer the questions that are put to you and not go into commentaries. The Prosecutor knows what he wants to elicit as answers, and that's what the Court will hear. And you may feel that you would like to talk lengthily about all kind of matters, but please restrict yourself to answering the questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could you turn, please -- in the English, it's page 5 of this report, and it's a paragraph which is headed "The accommodation of prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In the English, it's page 5, and I think that in the B/C/S it's headed "page 2" at the top, and it's a paragraph at the bottom of that page which I think is headed "The accommodation of prisoners of war." Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an inspection that takes place in November, and I'm going to read you what this individual has recorded, and then I'm going to ask you whether it fits in with your experience in the Heliodrom. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "In the said facilities, there are 2.600 prisoners of war who are of the same category as the prisoners of war in the previous shelter ..." that's Gabela, we'll look at that in a moment, "... of the same category; i.e., real prisoners of war have not been separated - members of the BH Army have not been separated from civilians who have been brought 'for various reasons.'" And I think in both languages that's in inverted commas. All right? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I want to stay on the topic of the people that you met both in Heliodrom and in the other detention facilities. This report also deals with who was in Gabela. All right? And if you turn back in the report, it's the English page 3, and in the B/C/S it's the first page with text on it before page 1, do you have that? That's it, back one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command and control system in the shelter and security measures"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's the very first page that has text on it, and it's a heading "Situation of prisoners of war." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you, you follow with me in the B/C/S, if you would, what it says: "There are about 300 POWs in each of the said facilities. There are currently 1.268 prisoners of war. All prisoners of war are persons of Muslim nationality, male, and there are some of them - I've not been able to establish the figure precisely - who are under 18 and some who are above 60 years of age." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if you turn the page, please, we'll read the next paragraph, and then I'm going to pause and ask you if you can help us: "In brief personal contacts with prisoners of war, the impression is that many of them have been brought to the shelter from their homes, street, or work-places, while the rest have been captured during combat operations." Do you see those observations by the author of this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You told the Judges yesterday that you, yourself, had sat with the detainees in Gabela, that you had talked to them, and that you had even shared their food. Did you form the same impression as the author of this report about how they had come to be there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. So people who had been, some of them, taken from their homes, from the street, from their places of work, and locked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, should I answer again? Yes, a part were arrested, and as for these, I don't know if they were taken away for preventive reasons from their homes, or from some other reasons, I'm not able to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Just as --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in any case --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the last word the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I think the interpreter wanted you to finish your sentence, and I'm happy for you to do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sorry. I said as for those who were arrested in combat, yes, that goes, but I was told that for some security reasons, some people were brought in to that place, so this was for preventive reasons and for reasons of potential retaliation. But regardless of that, I condemned the act of taking people away from their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You thought it was wrong at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with one correction. If we're not talking about the people who fired at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. You met a range -- you, yourself, met a range of different people in the various camps that you visited, didn't you, people of different backgrounds, different walks of life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to ask you to use the term "prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We'll use the term "prison," of course, sir. In Dretelj, you met a doctor. He gave evidence to this Trial Chamber. He had the pseudonym DD, and he gave evidence that he had met you because he was discussing his fear about a jaundice epidemic. Do you remember a conversation with a doctor in Dretelj who was worried about jaundice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I spoke with all the doctors. As for that doctor, I don't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about all the doctors at the moment. I'm asking you about the doctor in Dretelj who was worried about a jaundice epidemic. You don't remember him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there were five doctors there, and I spoke with all of them, so I don't know which one it was. But, sir, I can tell you there was no jaundice. I said that yesterday, and thank the Lord that in all the areas that I was in charge of, there was no single epidemic of an infection disease. And I would have been glad to hear someone say something like that, because that would mean that they were helping me in my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're agreed there was no jaundice. That individual, DD, told this Court that he was being fed on leftover food and that he lost 30 kilos in his body weight; a doctor, like you. Do you recall now meeting somebody who was imprisoned and being fed badly so that they started to lose weight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said yesterday that on the basis of the story not of this colleague of mine, but that the average weight loss was ten and a half kilos, according to what was said, I mean, we noted this yesterday, we dealt with that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm asking you a very specific question, whether you recall meeting this doctor who told this Court that he lost 30 kilos.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, thank you. You met a dentist in Gabela. You noted in one of your reports, and we can look at it if you wish, that the prisoner's teeth were bad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The prisoners had bad teeth, and there happened to be a dentist locked up in Gabela, and you were suggesting that it might be an idea to provide him with some dental equipment so that he could help to treat the people with bad teeth; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Bad teeth being a common side effect of malnutrition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When you're starving, you start to lose your teeth; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that means a deficiency in Vitamin C. A person can eat a lot, but if the food is not of sufficient quality, then you can suffer from scurvy. Why did sailors fall victim to scurvy? Because they had a lack of Vitamin C. But let me say something else, there was no dentist's chair in any of the barracks. No single HVO soldier had the opportunity of being examined by a dentist. In the same way, in the town of Mostar, I'm speaking about the town of Mostar, there was only one dentist who was working in the medical centre, and he didn't have any equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Witness BQ, who gave evidence in this case, told the Trial Chamber that he lost all of his teeth as a result of the food or lack of food that he received in Dretelj, and you saw people there with very bad teeth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also saw, did you not, that there were women detained in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First let me answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a "thank you." I don't know what he was thanking the gentleman for, but the transcript does not indicate that there was a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Mr. Karnavas is quite right. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You nodded, and you're going to need to say, "Yes," if you want to agree with the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I must answer that question, I must answer. This is not a pantomime. You're asking me, and you are allowing me to nod my head, but this is not something that I'm not permitting myself, mime. Anyway, if you permit. If you have read, and I hope that you have read -- I don't think that you have not read, and that you can see that in the reports it is specifically clearly written that the food is sufficient in quantity and quality. And it's sufficient, so -- the quantity was not sufficient, so there wasn't a sufficient supply of vitamins. In any case, it was an area affected by war, and if you read the reports, you will see that the amount of humanitarian help was very small and that both the refugees and the population was suffering from the same difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you nod your head -- you're doing it now. Do it just as you wish, but do answer the question with a "yes" or "no." Otherwise, we'll get into that sort of confusion and Mr. Karnavas will have to help us. I asked you the question whether you saw people in Gabela who had bad teeth, all right, and is the short answer to that, "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I must say I saw the same thing with a lot of soldiers who had come from the country and who did not have sufficient hygienic -- hygiene habits. You cannot compare a soldier from The Hague or a soldier from the country. Those soldiers who come from the villages don't have a habit of brushing their teeth and their hygiene habits are lacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. So just to summarise, you mentioned yesterday that the doctors helping the detainees in Heliodrom were themselves detainees; is that right? You gave us the name yesterday, Mr. Hadzic, who -- Dr. Hadzic, I shall call him, who was one of the Muslim doctors detained in Heliodrom; yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're nodding your head just very slightly there. Is the answer, "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you -- I'm not -- I'm asking you not to look at me nod my head, but to listen to my answer. I am just listening and nodding my head, but I think that it was a major thing that I did find Dr. Hadzic, who was a prisoner, and that I transferred him to the medical staff. He was my friend and colleague from the Vales Sports Club, and he no longer had the status of a prisoner. Quite the contrary, Dr. Hadzic went to town with a medical vehicle, and he would bring back medical supplies to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. In these camps, you saw doctors, at least one dentist, children, old people, and you knew that there were women; yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me. As far as women are concerned, I have to go back to the first testimony. I perhaps said at the time, because I was under stress, that I did not see -- for me, it's a crime that a child, anyone under 18, or above 60 to be there. I did not see any women. I believe that any kind of harming of the health or any kind of insinuation about women, I mean, I heard, I went, I was taken where they were supposed to be, but I didn't find any. But I did tell my superiors, if there are any, we need to do everything to remove those people from there. If you had read my reports, and you probably did, and I hope you studied them carefully, that it says four medical commissions and other commissions of -- so that people who are in vulnerable categories can be freed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. You weren't in any doubt that there were women in isolation? May I just finish this topic, and then I'll certainly give way. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No, no, no, colleague. I would just like to object to a previous question very briefly. I believe that the witness did not understand the question, and I think that the Prosecutor would need to clarify and put it a bit slower. We're jumping from one prison to another, and from what I have been listening of the testimony of the witness and from my study of the documents, I don't know how the Prosecutor can come to the plural, "Where did you see women?" I think the Prosecutor would need to take each prison case by case, "Did you see women in Heliodrom, in Gabela, in Dretelj, in Ljubusko," for each of these cases. So I think now the witness is quite confused and he doesn't know exactly which prison we are talking about now. I think that this would be quite a useful thing to do now, in the courtroom, to go from one prison to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, do try to be more specific when you put the questions, "Were these women in the Heliodrom, in Gabela, in Dretelj; according to you, where were they?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look at P 06924, in that case, and I'll make it clear I'm dealing with the topic of the people that this witness saw in the camps, before we look at the conditions, P 06924?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I have asked the question, you were aware that there were women there; all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into closed session, because this is a document signed by the witness. Please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In English --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counsel, Your Honour, for the record, we're back in open session. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's 10877. It's towards the back of the bundle. It's a very long exhibit. It's a transcript of the evidence that you gave in the Naletilic case in Tuta Stela. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I don't have this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, you do. That's it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this paper, please. No. In Croatian language, I don't have this paper, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You don't have an interpretation of it. I'm going to read to you a part of it. Everybody will follow. And if I read it incorrectly, someone will put me right. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you turn to page 14698 in the top right-hand corner, please, can you see there are page numbers in the top right-hand corner, "14698"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text is in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's in the English language, but the numbers will help you. 14698, and I'm picking up at line 17. You were being asked a question there by another Prosecutor in the Tuta Stela case about a part of your report that we have, in fact, already looked at today. It's part of your report of the 27th of November, P 06924, and I'm not going to take us back to it now. But you were asked this question: "Witness, I have a few more questions on that last paragraph, when it says: 'It was observed that the wards assigned to physical labour were mostly of normal weight because of increased food.'" And the Prosecutor then asked you this question: "Did you know that wards were taken out for physical labour?" That was the question that you were asked. Do you follow so far, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could you confirm that you follow my question so far, please, for the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I can hear it through the interpreter, and I am following you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to read what you said when you were asked that question. You said, and it's line 23: "I never saw that. I heard that some were taken. Personally, I said to my colleague, 'Bozic,'" that's Stanko Bozic, isn't it, "'Bozic tried to prevent this. It's a war crime.'" Can you see the answer that you gave in the Tuta Stela case there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "I asked where these people were. I met some people. And maybe for fear, or for other reasons, they told me they didn't go there." And then you said this: "Some kept quiet, and from that I understood that they were taken there. What they did, I don't know, but later on I heard that they had been digging trenches or what have you." Now, I just want to pause there. You're describing there, are you not, having heard that prisoners were being used for forced labour, and, quite rightly, sharing your concerns on that topic with the warden of the prison, Stanko Bozic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard, but I didn't see. This is a major difference. And, definitely, just the knowledge, as you can see, that I went -- and this is in answer to some of your previous questions to me. I'm not a salon doctor. I'm a doctor who went to the front-lines, who went among the prisoners. I went to ask. People were quiet. As a person and as a man, I understood that they were quiet, because at that point in time I was on the other side. If somebody was silent, I could only assume, and that assumption would be enough to initiate some reactions. And as for if I had ever seen, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, you make that clear, that you never saw it. But you were so worried about the situation that you spoke to Stanko Bozic, the warden, and informed him that it was a war crime and that he should try to prevent it happening; yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you knew a deal about war crimes, because I think as you also said yesterday, but mentioned in Tuta Stela, you had given lectures to the military police on the Geneva Conventions, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the aspect of special preventive medical protection. We're probably not thinking along the same lines. Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I work in preventive medicine, and I did carry the booklets that I had with me, and I gave them, because as far as I'm concerned, any person is a person. Without a prefix, they are a person. It doesn't matter. There is no gender, no prefix. As -- if that person is ill, that is all that I am taking into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I understand that. Can we look on at what you said next in that case. You said, and it's line 4 of the page that we were just on: "At that moment, I didn't have any personal knowledge, but I know -- I know that I told Dr. Bagaric that these people, if they existed, if they were taken for labour, that they had to be protected, because they were a product of a misunderstanding, and that was the worst form of maltreatment and harassment. If you have to do something against your better judgement, then that is the worst form of harassment." Can I ask you, please, when and where you told your colleague, Dr. Bagaric, about your fear that there may be forced labour within the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that it was going on, but that perhaps that it was going on. It's different, if something is going on or could be going on, at least it's in my language like that. English is something different. If you noticed, sir, I went to see everyone, from the front-line to those who were refugees. I was in the field. My first thing to do was to get to know people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I'm asking you about a conversation that you had with Dr. Bagaric. I'm not asking you about other conversations at the moment, and I'm entitled to ask you that question and to expect that you will do your best to answer it. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You said -- [Previous translation continues]... that you know, you know that you told Dr. Bagaric that these people, if they existed, they were taken for labour, that they had to be protected, and I want to know from you, if you can help us, when you had that conversation with Dr. Bagaric, and where you were when you had it, and any other details that you can help us with. Do you follow the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... then please tell us about the conversation with Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply -- my first meeting could have been only in the Health Sector, at our work-place. I said these are suspicions, and if there is a suspicion, then we would need to react. We, and through our superior institutions, we would need to overcome this. This is my first reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So when you -- when you told him of your fears, you believed that you were in the Health Sector, in your work-place, and you discussed with him how the problem could be overcome; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to overcome it, to find a potential solution that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What was done, then, please, by you, by Dr. Bagaric, or by other people within the Health Sector of the Defence Department, to get to the truth of this issue of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably do not remember, but yesterday it was said a number of times, and it was accentuated yesterday a number of times, that we are a consultative, advisory, educational organ, and we could only have written something, passed it on to the superiors to correct this. If you followed me yesterday and today, and especially yesterday, you could have noticed that the number of addresses where we sent our reports was larger because we, specifically the Health Sector, was not able to resolve this. This exceeds our competence. But, for example, we could have - and that was my duty and which does not absolve me - we could have prevented an epidemic. And I believed that it was my great responsibility there. In an overcrowded environment, you have an epidemic breakout very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You've made that position very clear to us about epidemics, but I'm asking you very specifically about forced labour, and I'd like to know from you, please, if a report on that topic was compiled by you and sent to anybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report, first of all, something was not seen. If something is not seen, I cannot write about it, if I'm unable to bring myself to the position of being an observer. So you saw yesterday that the number of addresses where we sent this report had increased, and we sent it even to the president of the republic. And probably, as you know, in this trial a person with the establishment post such as my own was not able to write to Mr. Stojic, but we did write to him. It should have gone to the establishment subordination, where I am the fifth or the sixth link, but evidently I did violate or exceed some of my authority in an attempt to resolve these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So you're -- can I be clear whether your evidence is that you believe you did write to Mr. Stojic in order to tell him of your fears, that there was forced labour in the Heliodrom, or is your evidence that you did not write to Mr. Stojic in order to tell him of those fears?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written to everyone, and it says to whom, if you look at it, if you look at the reports. You'll see that it went to Mr. Stojic, and the Main Staff, and the president as well. And let me repeat, once again, and I'm going to repeat this several more times, the medical service, medical corps, in all the armed forces throughout the world, is a professional body and a consultative body and working in the rear, and the function of which is to provide medical care, prevention, and so on, treatment, and providing material so that this can be carried out, and you have that in all countries in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. The institution that you were going into was one in which forced labour was taking place and detainees were being both killed and wounded as a result of that forced labour on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard, never saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you were dealing with Stanko Bozic, and you said that you had a conversation with him in which you said to him that he should try to prevent it. Shall we just look, you and I, and see what Stanko Bozic knew about the position immediately before your visit in September, what Stanko Bozic knew. If you look with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask - excuse me, Mr. Laws - a question that goes a bit back to what the witness has said a short while ago. Witness, you have said that you sent the report to everyone. Which report were you speaking about? That was on page 54, lines 6 and following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in all the reports, if they referred to prisons, you will be able to notice that the number of reports is large. There are a lot of reports. That's number one. Number two, if you notice that the same methodology of work and, three, if you find that at the end, what can happen, and, number four, who it was addressed to. So if you look at these reports chronologically, you will see that the number of addressees is increased; that is to say, we did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Witness, you are going a bit astray. The question was: There was this suspicion that you had, and you admit that you had a suspicion, that prisoners were taken from detention centres for forced labour, and you were asked did you report on this. And you said, I sent the report to everyone. But which report referred to this suspicion? That's my question. The rest, you say, I know very well, I can see myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, I can't remember exactly because there were so many reports, but I have to say, if you will allow me to do so, Your Honour, that I have to clear this up. When I testified the first time via videolink, I don't know why I was there. I just saw one or two examples. I was absolutely unprepared, and I don't remember the matter in hand at all. As a result, I got vitiligo and high blood pressure because it was extreme stress for me. So as a doctor myself, I tried to push that to the back of my memory, and I really don't remember. I was prepared inadequately. I was taken like a lamb to the slaughter, and not to this day do I know why that happened to me, and I don't remember that. And I asked Ms. Nozica yesterday -- she asked me when I was taken prisoner, and she said February, and I said, "Senka, but it was hot weather." So as a doctor, following Freud, I'm trying to push that to the back of my consciousness, so I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but that was not really the question. Here, today, you have said that you had this suspicion. It was only a suspicion; you haven't seen it. But you had this suspicion that prisoners were taken from detention centres for forced labour. If that really happened, you knew, and you told Ms. Bozic that would be a war crime. And you have spoken about these worries to Dr. Bagaric. And then you were asked, What happened then? Were the authorities informed of this suspicion? And you said, I sent the report to everyone. Now, perhaps I -- the whole answer was given by you, namely, that you simply do not remember which report that was. Do you then remember for sure that there was a report in which you stated these suspicions to "everyone"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I really can't remember, but I personally -- as a former soldier, one thing is certain, and I know that. If a superior talks to me, then what he says, as far as I'm concerned, they're orders to me. Now, you can understand that in one way or another. And I also know that if I, as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have answered my question. Please continue, Mr. Laws. I'm sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, I'm grateful for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you to look with me, please, at some documents that show us exactly what Stanko Bozic knew, the man that you were discussing this topic with. And if you would look first, please, at P 05324. All right? P 05324. Now, I make it clear to help you, sir. I'm not suggesting that you have seen this document before, but it is written by a man who you discussed this topic with, and I want to know what -- I want to look at what he knew whilst he was having that conversation with you. All right? Can you see it's signed by Stanko Bozic, and it says that on the 21st of September of 1993, the order of the 3rd Brigade took over four detainees for their work, and on the 22nd of September, "we were verbally informed that a detainee, Azim (son of Ibro) Karadjuz, got killed due to Muslim defence forces activities." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And this is nine days before you went into that same institution. If you turn on, please, two documents in your bundle, you'll have P 05343, and this one is dated the 24th of September, and again it's signed by Stanko Bozic, and again it's dealing with the death of detainees who have been taken for work. This time they were handed over for work to a military police officer in charge of their security, and his name is given. And on the 24th of September, so a week before your visit of the 30th, the prison were told that the two named individuals there had been killed by Muslim defence force action. Can you see that? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So the person that you were discussing the issue of forced labour with appears to have known very well that there was a problem in the prison and that people were being taken out and being killed; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that this is the first time that I see these reports, and I don't bring myself into any correlation with this, I see no correlation between me and this, and I reject that with indignation, military police and all the rest of it. That's the first point. Number two, I did not hear that these people had been killed, and there was talk of the fact that Mr. Bozic talked to me about forced labour, not about killing, if he indeed did mention that. But let's accept that he did, but that he talked about killing, I don't know, because there's no theoretical chance of me having seen this report, not even a theoretical chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I made that very clear, with respect to you, in my question, that you hadn't seen this report. Its significance is that the person that you were discussing forced labour with knew exactly what the position was, and I hope that that's not lost on you, sir. The prison, the Heliodrom, was providing labourers in very, very large numbers, including on the very day that you went there, the 30th of September. We don't have time to look at all of the documents that we have, but if you'd look at P 05489, we can see that in a document headed the 30th of September, one of the days that you went into the Heliodrom, 15 detainees were authorised to be taken out of the prison to perform work. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And we're not going to turn them all up there. They're all in the bundle, and for the record I can give the numbers of these documents, but it will be a waste of our time to look at them. They all start "05," and we've looked at 489. We can look also at 493, it's in my bundle, 507, 508, 510, 511, 512, 514. Those are all documents which deal with prisoners of war or detainees within the Heliodrom going out to perform forced labour on the 30th of September. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object, because no mention is made in the document of either prisoners of war or detainees. What the documents refer to that we've seen so far is "detainees." The word used is "detainees."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "Detainees," yes, that's right. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Not prisoners of war or prisoners, but "detainees" in absolutely all the reports. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I will happily accept that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: On the 30th of September, the documents that we have show that many, many dozens of detainees, to use that word, were being taken out from the Heliodrom, and it's the self-same day that you went to the Heliodrom. And I want to ask you whether, going into that institution, you were ever aware of people being taken for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that I have absolutely nothing to do with the sector of the defence of Mostar, nothing with these people here, and I really didn't know about this, and I -- and this seems to be quite up in the air, that I'm here being asked these questions. I did my work as a doctor, I dealt with medicine, and I can swear that I didn't see them. They could have gone at 7.00 and I might have come in at 9.00. They could have left at 5.00 and I could have come in at 1.00. So how can you link me with these people here? That is just mobbing. I don't know this person, this head of sector, or anybody here, so how do you bring me into correlation with this at all? I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, as I think I mentioned earlier, that the way this procedure operates is that I don't have to answer your questions at this stage. The Judges will decide. All right? You were going into that prison. You had a suspicion. It so happens that on that day many dozens of people were being taken to forced labour, and in the week before, some people being taken to forced labour had been killed. It's a fair question to ask you, don't you think, whether you knew, going into that institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I absolutely did not know about that. What Bozic told me, I said what should be done. Had I seen it, I would have put even greater effort into having the things done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Would you look with me, please, at document P 05503, your report of the 30th of September that we've looked at in another context. Can you see, in the B/C/S, at the foot of the first page of text, there are numbers 1, 2, and 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if you turn over the page in the B/C/S, and it's still on page 2 in the English, item number 4: "Transfer the seriously ill and wounded to the Mostar HVO War Hospital." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. You were keen that the sick and wounded in the Heliodrom should be transferred to a hospital where they could receive appropriate care; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's a wrong interpretation. Seriously wounded and seriously ill, there were none of those. Now, at the level of Heliodrom, under number 3, to form an infirmary, so that is general medical care and attention, but higher in quality. Now, people to be treated in hospital, secondary treatment and tertiary treatment, the tertiary level of medical treatment in hospital. So this was a committee made up of these people listed above. It was of the -- of the Health Sector, and we certainly didn't see -- at least I didn't see this, and that's why we say that an infirmary should be set up and that any seriously sick or wounded persons should be transported to hospital. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me just try to help you, if I may. You're talking there about the need for people who require hospital treatment to receive it, and I want to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I want to look with you at a letter written the very day before your visit by Stanko Bozic, whom you saw on the 30th of September, and see why -- why it might have been necessary to get those people to hospital. And if you turn in the binder, please, to P 05465, I can help you, sir, by saying, before you do, I hope, that this is not a document you've seen before, it's not addressed to you, nobody is suggesting that you know its contents, but it comes from Stanko Bozic to Brigadier Dr. Ivan Bagaric, a gentleman with whom you said you had a conversation about forced labour, and it is saying: "I'm sending you this letter to inform you about the difficulties and problems encountered regarding the treatment of some severely wounded and sick inmates due to inadequate accommodation, insufficient material, and medicaments. I would also like to ask you to transfer the sick persons mentioned above and enable them to be treated in a hospital." And it goes on to say: "The forthcoming visit of the International Red Cross Committee is yet another reason for the transfer, as it would prevent them from finding the sick in inappropriate accommodation and treatment conditions and consequently getting an unfavorable impression of the Heliodrom, which would be detrimental for the HVO and the Croatian people in general." That's the day before your report is saying "transfer the seriously ill and wounded to hospital." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And no doubt when you met Stanko Bozic on the 30th of September, he impressed upon you his view that these people, who were too ill to be in the Heliodrom, had to be moved out before the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the 14th of August, and I remember it well - you can look for it - Mr. Bagaric sent in an instruction where it states what everybody should do, in exact terms. Among other things, the 3rd Brigade -- the Medical Corps of the 3rd Brigade, that is, and the warden, should have all the seriously sick people who need specialised military -- medical assistance should be transferred to hospital in motor vehicles belonging to the brigade, the medical corps ambulance, and, if necessary, to the War Hospital as well, and this instruction was given a month and a half, I believe, before this. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me try --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you found that instruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me try to interrupt, if I may, before we talk in too much detail about the 3rd Brigade and ambulances. I think you and I might agree that there were people in the Heliodrom who badly needed to go to hospital, who were not being taken to hospital in September, and that action had to be taken. You and I can agree about that, I think, can't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if we just look back at your report, 5503, which is the one that insists or recommends that there be a transfer of the seriously ill and wounded people, we can see, on page 3 of the English and on page 2 of the B/C/S, that the people who are being sent copies of this report include Mate Boban; Bruno Stojic, personally; it says - yes - Zarko Tole; your senior, Dr. Ivan Bagaric, personally; and the officer for prisoner exchange, Mr. Brko Pusic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And item 7 on the same report, it's a little bit further up the page in the B/C/S and at the very top of the page in English, it says this: that you want to be informed -- you want the Defence Department Healthcare Sector to be informed on the undertaking of the above measures by midday on the 1st of October, and you give a fax number for them to communicate whether they have complied with your instructions. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have this attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've just had a look at this. Item 5, at least in the document that I have -- I don't know what documents I have anymore. P 05503, under point 5, this commission states: "... organisation of clearing up the surroundings and the interior of the centre." Now, whether it's Bagaric, or Bruno Stojic, or whoever to react --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I've not asked you a single question about organising the perimeter or cleaning anything. I'm dealing with ill people who need to go to hospital, and you know that full well. And if I may, respectfully, ask you to stick with the topic. I'm going to ask you to turn to your report, which is in our bundle at P 06924. 06924. In September, people needed to go to hospital, and I want to see what the position was in November and whether it had got any better. And we looked at this document in a slightly different context earlier today, and we clarified that the list of people at the foot of page 3, when Judge Antonetti was asking you questions, those are all people who were detained. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it's a long list of people who have no place whatsoever in a prison, do they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Eighteen mentally-ill people; people who have suffered heart attacks; people with grade L myasthenia, a muscular weakness; osteomyelitis, I think is a bone infection. Over the page, 55 people recovering from wounds, in a setting completely unsuited for their care. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you look at what it says underneath that, this is what it says: that this list was compiled by doctors who worked there, specifically Muslims. And then if you look at the list, you have some ludicrous medical things there. There is a correction of sight. I mean, who doesn't need to have their sight corrected? But I accept the list -- accepted the list, and it went further on, it was sent further on so that we could help. Now, if we were to look at -- for a list in February, then you'll see the situation. And thanks to the pressure from us and all the things that we wrote, the situation did improve. So my conclusion would be that the people here -- it's like this: Anybody who said anything, whatever they said would be recorded. If somebody said they were slightly deaf, that would be recorded. That's not an illness, being slightly deaf, impaired hearing, but we'd write it down anyway. And I think I said that sometimes I hypertrophied or, rather, inflated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, you said that. Thank you. But the true position was that although you had correctly identified the problem in September and had asked that urgent action be taken, for whatever reason, come November, people who should have been in hospital were still in the Heliodrom, and it is as simple as that, isn't it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, I think we're not disagreeing, you and I, over very much of this. Can I ask you, please, to look at something with me in one of your reports. 05503 is your report for the Heliodrom in September. 05503.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the commission's report, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You're one member of a commission of three; is that the point that you want us to understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can you help us, please. At the very top of the document, we have a list of features that have been established by the inspection, and the inspection established, number 1: "On entering the centre, we were not challenged; nor were our papers checked by authorised persons." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And number 2: "The number of men physically securing the centre is inadequate." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the centre surroundings and the centre itself are untidy and neglected; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- why you, as a doctor, and as you told us yesterday, only concerned with the well being of the detainees, why is security now something that makes an appearance in your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because of the safety and security of these people. Security was a question for me. There were numerous extremists, people who for this or that reason had lost someone, or they were in prison, and we were personally afraid. If we can go in just like that, anyone else can go in, they can do whatever unpleasantness they like. They can also bring in biological agents. And I believe that in prisons anywhere in the world, there should be security, and there evidently was no adequate security here. I mean, we can compare. In regular circumstances, I would be stopped, never mind in wartime situation. And as far as I'm concerned, regarding the situation of the prisoners and the security, the commander of the 3rd Brigade should have been punished for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: What was damaging the health and well-being of the people in the Heliodrom was the fact that they were locked in, not that they needed more guards; that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially true. They were detained for such and such reasons, and the guards were supposed to prevent, as Lenin said, the fools in our ranks from doing some harm to them. That was supposed to be the general idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you some questions about Dretelj, please, which is a prison to which you went on these three days in August of 1993, according to your report, and I want to get the dates clear with you. It's the 17th of August, the 18th of August, and the 26th of August. On those three days, you went to Dretelj; yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I have the transcript. Can I have the report or something? If you allow me, this was 15 years ago. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's 2D 00278, and you will find there the days that I have just given you for the visits that you made to the Dretelj prison, using the word that you prefer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You're very welcome. I want to show you some pictures, please, that were taken on or about the 28th of August, 1993. They are pictures of people who had been released from Dretelj on or about the 28th of August of 1993, and they are an exhibit in this case. They have Exhibit number 04588, and I believe that they are on e-court, and I'd like to look at some of them with you, please. If we could -- that's number 1. If we could just move through to number 2. Number 3. Number 4. Number 5. Number 6. Number 7, please. Number 8. Number 9. And number 10. We don't have time to do all 93. You were in that camp, Dretelj, that those men -- some of those men came from days before these photographs were taken, sir. Did you see the people who were suffering in that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. But I see number 96. That is my first neighbour. I definitely did not see this, and this is horrible. I saw some other images when they were coming from the left bank, but this does not justify anybody doing something like that, especially us, from what we did in Dretelj. I'm not looking at what the other side did. I'm only looking at what we did. But this is my neighbour, and I still see him today. I absolutely condemn that. On the other hand, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let me make it clear. The gentleman that we still have on the screen in the photograph ending "96" was a neighbour of yours who we can see --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- has been reduced to -- what would you use to describe his condition? A pitiable figure; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you, sir, said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Cachexia, cachexia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The translation I'm getting is the same word that you're saying, so it may be that there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: A pitiable figure, and I think you were saying that what happened in Dretelj was something about which you were ashamed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Any normal person would be ashamed of that cachexia. Let me explain. It's a medical term. I don't know your legal language. It's malnutrition, excessive thinness, the Biafra syndrome, people who are very immunologically run down, who can be overcome by any illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, I would like to say again that I did not see these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you were in the camp the week before, and we're going to look at your report, which we've just turned up, 2D 00278. You're talking there about making sure that the food's prepared properly and that things are clean, and the chlorine's in the water and, over the page, that ambulances are equipped, and that people who are in need of emergency medical specialist aid are given it. There's not a line there about the people in Dretelj are starving to death, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I didn't see them. What I don't see does not exist for me. What I see, I write. I can suspect that something exists. In any case, sir, Mr. Prosecutor, you can look who this was addressed to. It was sent to the Office of the President of the HZ-HB.
