In normal army structure, a person who is 15 hierarchal steps below is unable to send anything higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... telling us about that again. I think I only have a few minutes remaining. SO we have that on the transcript. Thank you. I want to ask you just a few more questions, if I may. The conditions in Dretelj you told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I remember these photographs because we have already seen these photographs in the presence of other witnesses. You are a doctor, and you saw what their condition was. On the 28th of August, you prepare a report, and you say that after having conducted an investigation on the 17th, 18th, and 26th of August, you offer a number of solutions. But the state of health of these people was such that, normally speaking, you should have clearly mentioned the fact that they were so thin and that they required treatment. Nothing is mentioned about this in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not see those people. I went there where the commander sent me. If it was Dretelj, it was Dretelj. If it was Gabela, it was Gabela. It was Heliodrom, Heliodrom. That's where I went. I didn't see that. But I'm saying this is disgusting. It's horrible to see, it's terrible. I condemn this, regardless of the fact that they were in Dretelj, regardless of where they were. This is something to be condemned. People like this are in need of urgent medical help.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to look at the second photograph again, please. Doctor, when you see a person looking like this, from a medical point of view, what do you have to say about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terrible conclusions. These people were brought to the brink of desperation, physically and mentally. Physically, it's evident, but I believe in the -- in the terms of their mental state, it must be even worse. This is disgusting. I don't know what to say. These people would need to be placed urgently in hospital, and they would need to be given quite aggressive treatment to be saved. We always wrote about that, "increase quantities and qualities of food." I would be a criminal if I didn't say something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, this person, for instance, you didn't see him in that condition, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, never. I went where I was taken. Where I was taken, the situation was not like this. What I saw was what I wrote. Again, I note each of my reports says where, what, how, but each of my reports placed me in a kind of danger from the extremist forces. I was followed by the SIS, as an ex-soldier. This is terrible. This is something that you can only see in Africa. This is a monster and a criminal, whoever can do that. Even if he was my brother, he would still be a monster and a criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm taking some time, which will not be to your credit. Witness, I hope you can -- you can explain something, because I see that you were, during three days, August 18th -- 17th, 18th, and 26th, you say you conducted an investigation. Now, I can hardly imagine that you conduct such investigation without contacts with inmates, the very persons you were called to protect, as you have said several times. Now, how can it be explained that you didn't see any of the rather many that we have seen on the pictures? You have said you went where you were taken. Does that mean that it was the wardens of the prison who determined where you went and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally, yes. But I asked, if you remember in the case of Gabela yesterday, that I entered the hangar among the people, I closed the door, and I tried to find out as much as possible. But I am telling you also, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, that thanks to persistent reporting and touring, I did manage to form an infirmary and a medical station to these people. I didn't -- I wasn't able to see something that wasn't -- that I wasn't shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's not be led astray. I'm sure you are aware that if you visit -- if you want to seriously visit a prison, the first rule is that you determine what and whom and where you want to see something. But it seems that you felt not free in this respect, but were, yourself, scared of -- I put it a bit bluntly, that you were scared of finding out an unpleasant truth, because you thought you had SIS in your back and it might have negative consequences for you, personally, if you reported an unpleasant truth. Is that a misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am afraid I really need to object to this manner of question. This is really a construction that I believe is impermissible, so I object to this manner of questioning, because I believe that regardless of what the witness talked about, he's clearly stated and -- sufficiently clearly stated why he was the subject of SIS surveillance; because he was a member of the JNA, not because he worked -- he did his job. So I think this manner of constructing a question, as far as I am concerned, would be something that is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I'm going to answer, Your Honour. I believe that I should answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. And in the meanwhile, Ms. Nozica is invited to look at page 72, lines 19 to 24 or to 23, because that's what I -- that's the foundation for my question. The witness said: "I note each of my report, I was followed by the SIS as an ex-soldier." Yes, Ms. Nozica, Mr. Karnavas, someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, if I may, Judge Trechsel, I did hear the gentleman indicate that he believed he was followed by SIS. However, your construction of what you believe he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I made a hypothesis. I did not say I believed he said something. I'm trying to understand, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, well, because the way I understood his testimony was not that he was willfully trying to be blind to incidents. You know, that's what it appears your hypothesis is. But the gentleman indicated he's willing to answer the question, and I think we should allow him to answer the question. But I don't -- if your understanding is that's what he said, you know, I would disagree, but if that is a hypothesis, then obviously you're entitled to put the hypothesis there. You're putting it to the witness, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's exactly what it is, and absolutely nothing else. I'm just trying to find out. I have a personal experience in visiting prisons, many prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I know what one does. Now, the witness has not done this, apparently, and I would like him to explain. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be confrontational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I'm sorry if I have upset you, Ms. Nozica. That was not my intention, perhaps I have not been careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, one moment, please. I don't agree with what you said a while ago, for the following reason: The Judges are like doctors, we try to get to the truth, and sometimes we grope around. When a doctor is faced with a patient who is coughing, he may imagine that the patient is suffering from influenza, from tuberculosis, from a lung tumor or an infection or something else. Therefore, the physician must put questions to understand what the patient is suffering from. Well, the Judges do the same. They make assumptions and try to get to the truth. We are faced here with someone who has seen or who hasn't seen the prisoners, and we try to understand why he did not see any prisoners. An assumption is made, maybe he didn't see the prisoners because he may have been exposed if he had taken this too far. This is a valid question for a competent judge. Your objection, therefore, is lacks foundation and lacks sense. Why did the witness not go and see the prisoners? And the Judges don't understand why it is that if he saw the prisoners, some prisoners were [indiscernible]. This is in the interest of your client that we're trying to understand. There is nothing worse than Judges who don't put any questions. This is what I wanted to tell you, Ms. Nozica. Witness, can you answer this question put to you by my colleague? I agree 100 per cent with what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him answer the question, and then you can talk afterwards. Let your witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- thank you, Judge Antonetti, for the explanation. First of all, I can see that you have dealt with the subject well and you have read the reports. Often, I wrote a lot of ugly things. Had I been afraid, I would not have written down any of them. All of my reports mostly had negative connotations and would not be written by somebody who is afraid. I knew I was being followed by the SIS, I was told that, but I wrote from my conscience. I am a doctor. Just like you are a judge, I am a doctor by conviction. Number 2, I knew that I should be looking for this, this, and that. I don't know the localities. They went to different places. They took me there. The first thing was for me to see, physically. It's true, the doctor should take a diagnosis, a history of illness, and that's what I did. I saw all sorts of people in front of me, and specifically there are reports that I made efforts and that there was a kitchen in Dretelj where the wards were working, which was my personal doing. If necessary, I'm going to repeat a million times, Your Honours, I did not see these people, and I am horrified by these photographs. And if there is a fault within me, I accept that, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not have any problem with the question in the way that you put it. I remain by my objection. I believe that - this is my objection - that a Judge cannot put a hypothesis that would include a leading question, a suggestive question. If you wish to ask this witness, "Were you afraid of someone and did you write down all that you saw," that is quite all right for me. I believe that the question, the way His Honour Judge Trechsel put it, was a leading question, in my view, full of constructs, suggesting to the witness that he was not doing his job because he was afraid of something. And I still believe that these questions are impermissible. The way in which you interpreted it, Judge Antonetti, is quite acceptable, as far as I'm concerned, and the witness has answered the question in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you have explained to us that you didn't see them. Fine. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: May I end, please, sir, in the way that you and I began, that you said that it was a very unpleasant life experience for you to go into the Heliodrom, and does the same apply for your visits to Gabela, to Dretelj, and to the other detention camps, or "prisons," as you prefer, that the HVO were running?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a traumatising experience for me, when I found expelled people in the Students' Hall, children of three to four months, who were being breast-fed. All this is very traumatic. I think that us doctors also who went through the war also suffered suffer from PTSD as a result of that. So the negative experiences do not only have to do with camps, prisoners and so on, but also for places where there were refugees. It was a horrible thing. They were in their bare feet, with ripped clothes, arriving with bleeding feet, women with small children. This is something that I saw in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. If anybody wants to ask you about Kupres, they can do that. I'm asking you about camps, and I don't think there's any disagreement between you and I. What you saw in those HVO prisons appalled you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we must broaden it. Other things are awful, too. We cannot selective, we cannot pick selective questions. For me, it's horrible to see expelled people in one place, bleeding women, and three-month-old babies who are crying. Perhaps that can be an even greater trauma, but prison is also a trauma, for sure, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In some regards, we can be selective, because we can deal with one topic at a time. The topic that I have been asking you about so far is prisons, and I think you agree with me that what you saw in the HVO prisons appalled you and has left you to this day likely to start to cry when you recall what you saw; that's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'm going to object --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask that the witness be allowed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object because we're not in front of a jury.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can see if we we're in the Old Bailey, where we're trying to evoke emotion in front of the jury --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to evoke emotion. I'm trying to ask the witness a question which he's perfectly capable of answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm entitled to make my record, sir. Kindly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You forget something. You were not here yesterday. Yesterday, the witness displayed some considerable emotion. Therefore, the Prosecutor's question is to be seen in that context. And so if you were not present, you may not know everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that I know everything. I do know one thing, though; that the gentleman has said today, at least 50 times, how he was appalled, how he was horrified, and so on and so forth. How many more times do we need to hear it, especially were I'm being told repeatedly that I'm in front of professional judges, not an Iowa jury or not an Arkansas jury?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm summarising the position as this witness saw it in the camps that he went to. He's capable of answering the question, and there's no proper objection to it at all. I'd invite the Court to direct that he answers it. I think he wants to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I'm going to repeat the same. It's appalling and disgusting to me to see refugees, in the same way that it's appalling and disgusting to see a prison. There is no difference. These are people in misery who need material and psychological support. Sir, if you are making a difference between refugees and these others, sir, then you surprise me. You surprise me as a lawyer, as a person who works here, who sits there. You have really surprised me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor has just completed his cross-examination. Ms. Nozica, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regardless, I'll ask the witness to calm down. If he needs to drink some water or needs to take a break, I think -- anyway, I think it would be a good idea to take a break at this point, because I see that the witness is very upset. And all I need is 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you do with a break, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, just go ahead. Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't feel comfortable, questioning the witness after that reaction. I don't feel comfortable with it. And if the witness begins to have a flood of emotion, his floodgates of emotion break through during my questioning, I don't want to experience that. So, if possible, I'd like us to take a short break, and I don't have many questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Nozica, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, I haven't prepared the documents, and I'm going to put several to you, but I think that you can find it on e-court, on your screen, so let's look at P 4186 now, please, which is a document that the Prosecutor showed you, and it will come up on e-court so you'll be able to see it on your screen. It is in the Prosecution binder, but as I can say -- as I said, you can follow it on the screen. So this is a letter dated the 14th of August, and you said that you don't know whether Mr. Stojic received it. And it talks about food for these 2.100 detainees. Now, the Prosecutor put it to you that you could have known about this situation on the basis of document 2D 917, so can we have that document put up now - 2D 917 is the number - which is your own report dated the 6th of August. That is eight days before the other one. It is from the Heliodrom locality. Can we take a look at the second page of that document, which is also on page 2 of the English version. At the very top of that page, at the top of page 2, you can see the date, first of all, and then at the top, in the Croatian version, I think it is paragraph 4 of the English text, where the Central Investigatory Prison is talked about, and they say that the detainees get their food from the central kitchen. And my question to you is this, Witness: Doing your visit, did Mr. Bozic tell you anything about the problems of the central kitchen and that it was not able to supply food to all the detainees and prisoners in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Mr. Bozic said anything, then rest assured that it would have been written down, and I would have tried to solve the problem at least in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, during the examination-in-chief, I asked you something about this next subject that I'd like to address, and you said something about it in cross-examination, what the food that the HVO ate, was like, what they received. And in response to a question from the Prosecutor, you said that the members of the HVO, after eating the food in Heliodrom from the central kitchen, that they could also eat food at home. Now, I'm not going to ask you what food you had at home, but I would like to ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber the circumstances and conditions under which the members of the HVO lived, by and large, at least the ones that you came into contact with; that is to say, those who were not put up in barracks, or those who were, but generally where the people were who were not put up in the barracks, because you visited the front-lines. So tell us under what conditions they lived under and what food they ate, what kind of food they had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, we must distinguish between two categories of soldiers here. The first category are domicile soldiers, as we referred to them, that is to say, locals who lived there, who had their homes there, and where they never had a food shortage. But there was another category and a larger category --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just be precise. You said they had their homes, their houses, and as far as I understood you, did you say they had less food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were two categories. One was domicile soldiers, and the second category was soldiers who had become activated when they arrived in Mostar, having been -- having come from elsewhere. So this other category of people who had been expelled from the places they had lived beforehand had collective accommodation, and their situation was very bad. They had very little food, and unfortunately among them there were many people who later on imbued alcohol. And I personally think that their food was very bad, and not only for them, but the supply to their families too. And the second category were the category of people who lived there, if they lived around Citluk, Hamzici, Siroki Brijeg, Tucanovici [phoen], those places, they had better living conditions. So that was the situation, two categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the people who lived in Mostar. Were there enough collective centres in Mostar to accommodate them, people who had been expelled or arrived as displaced persons or refugees, to live in those centres with their relations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were centres of that kind, and the conditions there were indeed very poor, because there was a food shortage, there was very little food, and you must understand the situation. And with the influx of expelled persons into Mostar, the food storages had either -- had been depleted because they'd either been looted or whatever. I said that there was very little water, too, and that you had a lot of people in different ages in one place suddenly. There were many pregnant women, a lot of elderly persons, and there was generally very little food, and not only very little food for them but also for the domicile population, if we're all referring to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, yes, as the report refers to Heliodrom, I am referring to the domicile population of Mostar. Now, regardless of what you said in respect of Mostar, I'd like you to look at the next document, which is 2D 2021, and it will come up on our screens on e-court. Just wait for it a moment. I'll remind you that it is the report of the 6th of February, 1993, which is a weekly report. Now, I'm interested in the last paragraph there, where you talk about -- well, you say that when you toured an area, you found that effective action was necessary because there was serious shortcomings which needed to be dealt with as soon as possible. At the central kitchen in Ljubuski, you say existed, and the Jajce Battalion, Sutka and Tomislavgrad. Now, could you explain to Their Honours whether that was one of the localities in which the Jajce Battalion was located, the Tomislavgrad SUP, and could you tell us what the living conditions there were like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the one hand, we have the kitchen in Ljubuski, which was a domicile kitchen used by the people of Ljubuski. They cooked the food there and sent the food out to their soldiers. And if normal standards applied, you would have to close that kitchen, but there was no other way about it and you had to keep it going. Now, as far as your second question is concerned, the Tomislavgrad Vocational School, which was where the battalion was located, although these terms are all suspect, but, anyway, there were terrible conditions there because they -- there were families of refugees there, people from Jajce. You had the Krajl Tomislav Brigade members from Tomislavgrad and you had their families there as well, and there were a lot of them. There were not enough toilets, and one of the main tasks was to disinfect the area for the sewage and so on, to prevent the spread of typhoid and infectious diseases generally. And typhoid did break out in a part of Jajce or, rather, the people that fled in the face of the Serb aggression from Jajce. The conditions were terrible, and I'm sure you won't misunderstand me when I say that they might have been just a little better compared to the prison. Well, for the sole reason that there was no security there, that might have been the only difference, no guards, but otherwise the picture was very desperate and, of course, they drank a lot, so this made the situation worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now you've explained to us how they came to there from Jajce, but we were discussing the food and the soldiers -- nutrition for the soldiers and so on. Can you tell us specifically whether you were ever at that facility and what the soldiers' food was like and the food of the families that lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very insufficient, both in terms of the quality and quantity, it was no good at all. And then later on, after a long period of time had gone by, when I went back to my department, many people came for treatment from those parts, and they suffered from various syndromes, and many of them had chronic intestinal diseases. And I believe that in 1998, there was another epidemic of typhoid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, it seems to me that you are going a bit beyond and outside of what the questions of the Prosecution in cross-examination were. Jajce was not mentioned, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no mention was made of Jajce, but the members of the HVO Army was mentioned and their food. The people from Jajce later on became members of the HVO, so I'm talking about the conditions that prevailed precisely with respect to the application of the Geneva Conventions, so I'm talking about the state of food that the HVO had. And these members from Jajce, as we can see from this report, without a doubt, were members of the HVO, there's no doubt about that, on the 3rd of February. And I asked this witness in general terms, this document being merely an illustration of what the witness has already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm only focusing on food here, on the food situation. Before the break, you began to speak about refugee centres. Could you explain to us whether you toured these refugee centres on a regular basis, whether they existed all over HZ-HB? And I'm specifically asking you about the refugee centres where there were Croats. And then could you explain to us what kind of food they had and what the state -- their living conditions were during this period of time? Let's take it from the end -- from May 1993 to the beginning of 1994, for instance. To the best of your knowledge, what were their living conditions like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said yesterday that, well, through force of circumstance, I became a preventive medicine expert. I'm an infectologist otherwise. But as there were no specialists in preventive medicine and epidemiologists, I took it upon myself to perform that task. Had there been an epidemiologist present, he might have done the work better than me, but I know that I worked a lot, I worked very hard, and I think I satisfied the lack of knowledge that I might have otherwise had in the field, because I had to educate myself in preventive medicine. And as a former officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, I knew what had to be done. And I said yesterday that wherever you have a large number of people gathering together, regardless of where they are, they become potential sources of infection. And you know that during the winter, when a flu is prevalent, one of the preventive measures is to prevent large numbers of people conglomerating, to prevent the spread of disease, just as infectious disease, you have to separate the people and look at their accommodation. So wherever the refugees were accommodated was a signal to me to go and check out the conditions and situation, to do everything in my power to prevent these people from coming down with disease.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a minute, Witness. Your answer is a little too long, and I was focusing on one point, actually, and it is this: Were there refugees -- such refugee centres from May 1993 to the beginning of 1994 in the area of Mostar and the surrounding parts? And if so, did you visit them or it, and what was the food situation like for those refugees who were predominantly Croats? That's who I'm asking about, the Croats. And I know that you said yesterday that you visited the refugee centres which had Muslims in them at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I made several visits, not one but several, and there's a lot of paperwork to bear that out. There was not enough food at the beginning of the war, when the roads were cut off, the communication lines were cut off, and when food couldn't be brought in. There was not enough food for the domicile population either. And as for the localities you are asking about, the people were certainly hungry there. They certainly didn't have enough clothing, and they certainly didn't have enough footwear. They didn't have enough hot water. They didn't have enough blankets or things to cover themselves with. They slept on the floor with the odd rug or blanket. We managed to clean them and disinfect them from time to time, but not very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, when you visited centres like that, you made your recommendations for improving the situation, did you not, and you indicated to the authorities under whose authority those centres were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I explained all that yesterday. I do not make a distinction between soldiers and civilians. As far as I'm concerned, they're all human beings, so I don't distinguish between prisons and displaced persons, expelled persons. I don't make that distinction, as I told the Prosecutor earlier on. I don't -- all I can distinguish is sex, age, and whether a person is healthy or sick. There's no other difference, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now let's move on to the next question, which relates to the genders. And the Prosecutor asked you whether you had seen women in Heliodrom. I am going to ask you this: Do you know whether women, too, could have been members of the BH Army, whether women could have been the perpetrators of certain criminal acts? And I'm referring to -- when I ask you this, I'm referring to your answer to that same question, the answer you gave in the Naletilic/Martinovic trial on page 14708, where you address that matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're asking whether women could? All I can say is that I didn't see them, but why not? Why could not a woman be that? And I -- when I was a child, I learnt about national heroes, women like Marija Bursac, who were partisans, and in my unit there were many women who -- and in the medical corps and quartermaster corps, and especially women up at the front-line, they were of no lesser value than their fellow combatants. But I don't think that a woman's place is in the army, but more in the rear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, you said you didn't see any women, and I am referring to the answer you gave in the Tuta Stela trial, so I'm asking you whether women can be army members, and can women be the perpetrators of criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that if there were women in the HVO, why wouldn't there have been any women in the Bosnian or Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can a woman perpetrate a crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any person, regardless of their race, age, gender, or sex, and regardless of their title, can make a -- commit a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I am going to show you now P 5464. You were talking about this document yourself, so I would like to ask you something about it. Can we look at this document in e-court, please. This is document 5465. My mistake. 5465. Witness, you haven't seen it yet. You're going to get it in a minute. Just one moment. The usher has found it. And you also have seen the document before. Please, you said that you don't know. This is a document that Mr. Stanko Bozic writes to the deputy of the defence head, Dr. Ivan Bagaric, and he complains in this document that the wounded and the sick should be transferred to hospital. You said yourself, and this is written in page 68, line 8 of our transcript of today, that you know that practically one month before that, Mr. Bagaric gave a precise instruction about how the sick should be transferred who are in need of hospital care; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you to look at document, and the document that was shown to you yesterday by my colleague, Ms. Alaburic, and this is document P 4145. It's going to come to you in the electronic courtroom. Just one moment, just wait, please. I just would like to ask you. You notice the date, the 14th of August, and now I'm going to just ask you if you -- if you had ever referred to this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Defence Counsel Alaburic put the question to me about this, but it was a bit terminologically demanding, this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at this last item, which says: "Until we resolve the issue of an ambulance for Heliodrom, please use vehicle OZJIH and the War Hospital of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the Operations Zone of the 3rd Brigade, where Heliodrom was, and they were given the option of so-called evacuation to them, so that the War Hospital would send vehicles, the vehicles would be loaded into the vehicles [as interpreted], and then they would be returned. This is evacuation to them. There is evacuation away from them, meaning that vehicles of the 3rd Brigade and the operation zone would take the prisoners and take them to the hospital. There would be two-way evacuation that would be used, to yourself and away from yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the documents, it says that Mr. Bozic received very precise instructions about the way in which you could send the ill to the hospital, those who required medical attention or hospital attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the 12th of August, well, it's a month and a half. I think the instruction is quite clear. Rather, it was foreseen that some unpleasant kind of situation could occur and that immediately, at the start, we would need to find a solution, because - you know what? - in peace time you mostly work on the basis of some assumptions. In war, not only are you operating with assumptions, but you have to make guesses, so it's even more difficult. So it's a major thing for you to manage to assume that something would happen so that this would not happen later. That is why they were taking all these measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now my last question. When you were talking about proposals for measures, you said in the response to the question by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, you said that it was obvious that the situation was getting better, in terms of the time as time went by. Now, I am specifically going to ask you this: First of all, is this correct, and in the same way was the situation gradually improving, as far as food was concerned for the people in the collection centres, as well as the provisions for Mostar, and was the HVO Army in Mostar getting better food as time went by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that there is a report somewhere, if I'm not mistaken, in February 1994 precisely referring to Heliodrom. I think it was February 1994, yes, where it was achieved that - amongst other things - at that particular location, the ward said that the food was qualitatively good, that they had toilet paper, that they had sufficient food, and that their people who were working there were taking preventive measures. And for me, that is a major thing. And I also believe that to be a result of our pressure, our voluminous writing, and reports and so on. And in the way that things changed there, things changed for the better among the expelled persons. If you compare and you look at those reports, you are going to see large, large steps forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The third category was: Were the members of the HVO, as time went by -- did the situation and the conditions of their food supplies improve? When you went out into the field, did you see anything like that when you were touring the units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D-AB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the situation was improving. There was more food and there was better quality of food. And looking at it from the aspect of preventive medicine, there was something else. Already at the time, it was the case that doctors in Heliodrom and at the front were keeping records and protocols. We had managed to achieve a complete positive move forward. Had the war gone on longer, we would have met all the required conditions. Thank God it didn't last long, but had it gone on, we would have continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Your Honours, I have completed my examination of this witness, and I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had 25 minutes for your redirect, which will be subtracted from your time. Witness, I'd like to thank you for having come to testify at the request of Mr. Stojic's Defence counsel. I wish you a safe journey home, and I wish you well. Before you leave the courtroom, I would like the blinds to be dropped so that you can leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something? First of all, thank you very much for the professional attitude, although for me this is a very traumatic experience. I thank the Defence lawyers and the Prosecution. And, first of all, I would like to thank the Victims and Witnesses Service because they have done so much to make this time, which has been devastating, stabbed me right in the heart, and it was very traumatic for me, to make it easier. And I would like to be excused in the future, and I have very high blood pressure now, and if I am summoned to testify again, I really don't know if I am going to live through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but while the witness is still in the courtroom, I really must say that if the witness believes that there is my responsibility here because he is under stress here today, had I known that the witness would be in this situation, I would not have called him at all. And this is information both for you and the witness, and my apologies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's drop the blinds now, please. Ms. Alaburic, I believe you want to say something about a housekeeping matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just one request. Last week, you allowed the Defence of General Petkovic to prepare a reply to the answers submitted by the Prosecution and the Defence of Mr. Coric in relation to rights of the accused in the case of conflicting defences. On the same day after I submitted that request, we received the reply from Mr. Stojic's Defence, and I'm just asking permission for this reply of ours to refer to all three responses, so I'm asking for an expansion of your decision to the response of Mr. Stojic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been recorded on the transcript, and the answers will include all three Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, tomorrow we have another witness. That's fine. The witness is coming; yes? We can start with this witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The plan is -- well, the preparations are proceeding according to plan, and I don't expect to encounter any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Nozica. It's time to adjourn the hearing now. I wish all and every one a pleasant afternoon, and we shall meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00.
